body:
A major change in Buddhist sculpture

From around the 1st century CE, important centres of Buddhist art developed in Gandhara and Mathura. During the Kushana period, the human image of the Buddha became increasingly prominent.

Although both schools produced Buddha and Bodhisattva images, they developed different visual characteristics. Their differences reflect regional materials, established sculptural traditions and wider cultural contacts.

The Gandhara school

Gandhara occupied a region extending across parts of present-day northwestern Pakistan and adjoining Afghanistan. Its artistic traditions developed through interaction among local, Bactrian, Parthian and Hellenistic or Greco-Roman elements.

Characteristic features include:

  • Faces modelled with relatively naturalistic anatomical detail.
  • Thick, wavy or curly hair arranged in carefully defined strands.
  • Heavy monastic robes with clearly marked folds.
  • Strong treatment of the nose, eyes, forehead and facial surfaces.
  • Use of materials including grey schist and stucco.

Schist is a type of metamorphic rock suitable for carving. Stucco is a plaster-like material that can be modelled into sculptural forms.

The Buddha head from Taxila, dated to the Kushana period, is an important example of Gandhara's treatment of the face and hair.

The Mathura school

Mathura in present-day Uttar Pradesh developed a strong sculptural tradition drawing on earlier Indian forms, particularly the modelling of yaksha figures.

Mathura sculptures commonly used red or mottled red sandstone. Important features of early Buddha images include:

  • Broad shoulders and a substantial, well-developed torso.
  • Rounded facial forms and relatively full cheeks.
  • More restrained treatment of the robe, sometimes leaving the right shoulder exposed.
  • Prominent halos and a strong frontal presence.
  • Figures that appear firm, balanced and physically vigorous.

The seated Buddha from Katra Mound, Mathura, dated to the 2nd century CE, is a representative example.

The Buddha sits cross-legged and raises his right hand in abhaya mudra, a gesture associated with reassurance and freedom from fear. The sculpture also includes attendant Bodhisattva figures.

Gandhara and Mathura compared

FeatureGandharaMathura
Principal regionNorthwestern Pakistan and adjoining areasMathura region, Uttar Pradesh
Common materialGrey schist; stucco also usedRed or mottled red sandstone
Stylistic influenceLocal traditions with Hellenistic and other western Asian influencesStrong indigenous tradition linked with yaksha sculpture
Human formDetailed facial modelling and defined anatomyBroad, rounded and substantial bodily forms
RobeProminent, deeply carved foldsComparatively restrained treatment

Buddhist iconography

Iconography is the identification and interpretation of images through characteristic attributes, gestures, symbols and associated narratives.

Buddha images may be recognised through features such as the ushnisha, a raised form on the head; elongated earlobes; a halo; monastic clothing; and hand gestures known as mudras.

Important Bodhisattva attributes include a lotus associated with Padmapani and a vajra associated with Vajrapani.

Mathura was not exclusively Buddhist. Its sculptors also produced Jain Tirthankara images, Hindu religious figures, yakshas, yakshis and portrait statues.

A distinction worth remembering

The Gandhara and Mathura schools should not be treated as if one was entirely foreign and the other completely isolated from outside influences. They belonged to interconnected historical worlds, but their surviving sculptures reveal recognisable regional approaches.

It is also misleading to assign the development of every early human Buddha image to one school alone. Both centres played major roles in the emergence and spread of anthropomorphic Buddhist sculpture.

Prelims focus

  • Gandhara and Mathura became major centres of Buddha-image production during the Kushana period.
  • Gandhara is associated with grey schist, strongly modelled faces and deeply indicated robe folds.
  • Mathura is associated with red sandstone and the earlier yaksha sculptural tradition.
  • The seated Katra Mound Buddha belongs to Mathura and is dated to the 2nd century CE.
  • Abhaya mudra signifies reassurance or freedom from fear.
  • Trap: Mathura sculpture included Buddhist, Jain and Hindu images, not only Buddha figures.

[Source: NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class XI, Chapter 4, 'Post-Mauryan Trends in Indian Art and Architecture', printed pp. 30–32 and 48–51.]

title: Gandhara and Mathura: The Development of Human Buddha Images

body:
Changes during the Gupta period

The Gupta period, broadly associated with the 4th–6th centuries CE, saw important developments in the representation of the human body, religious imagery and stone sculpture.

Compared with some earlier Kushana-period images, many Gupta sculptures emphasise a more restrained physical appearance, balanced proportions, gentle facial expressions and refined surfaces.

These developments are especially visible in Buddhist sculptures from Sarnath, while other regions produced important Hindu and Jain religious images.

The Sarnath school of Buddha sculpture

Sarnath, near Varanasi in Uttar Pradesh, became an important centre of Buddhist sculpture. Its association with the Buddha's first sermon also shaped the subjects represented in its art.

A celebrated seated Buddha from Sarnath, dated to the late 5th century CE, demonstrates the qualities of the Gupta-period school.

The sculpture is made from Chunar sandstone. The Buddha sits in a meditative posture, with his hands positioned in dharmachakra-pravartana mudra, representing the teaching of the doctrine.

The panel below the seated figure includes a wheel flanked by deer and associated disciples, identifying the event of the first sermon at Sarnath.

Stylistic characteristics of Sarnath

  • Fine modelling: The body is slender and carefully proportioned.
  • Soft facial expression: The face conveys calmness and concentration.
  • Transparent-looking robe: Drapery clings closely to the body.
  • Minimal robe folds: The garment is not represented through heavy, deeply carved ridges.
  • Refined surface: Outlines and transitions between bodily forms are delicate.

These features distinguish Sarnath from the heavier robe folds commonly associated with Gandhara sculpture and from some earlier, more substantial Mathura figures.

Important Buddha mudras

MudraMeaningRecognisable gesture
AbhayaFearlessness or reassuranceHand raised with palm facing outward
DhyanaMeditationHands resting together in the lap
BhumisparshaCalling the earth to witnessHand lowered to touch or indicate the earth
DharmachakraTeaching or turning the wheel of the doctrineHands held near the chest in a teaching gesture

Gupta-period Hindu sculptural themes

Udayagiri: The Varaha relief

The Udayagiri Caves near Vidisha in Madhya Pradesh contain important Gupta-period rock-cut sculpture. The celebrated Varaha relief in Cave 5 belongs to the early 5th century CE.

Varaha is the boar incarnation of Vishnu. The composition represents the rescue of the Earth, personified as a goddess, and brings together a large central figure with numerous surrounding forms.

The work demonstrates how a religious narrative could be carved into a monumental rock surface. It also shows that Gupta sculpture was not limited to independent standing or seated images.

Deogarh: Narrative panels of Vishnu

The Dashavatara Temple at Deogarh in Uttar Pradesh, associated with the late Gupta period, is an important example of early structural temple sculpture.

Its major sculptural themes include:

  • Sheshashayana or Anantashayana: Vishnu reclining on the serpent Ananta.
  • Nara-Narayana: The sages Nara and Narayana practising penance.
  • Gajendramoksha: A scene associated with Vishnu's rescue of Gajendra.

The temple doorway also includes representations of the river goddesses Ganga and Yamuna.

The temple is associated with a panchayatana plan, involving a principal shrine and 4 smaller corner shrines. This architectural arrangement is distinct from the iconographic subjects represented in the temple's reliefs.

Why Sarnath and Gupta sculpture matter

Gupta sculpture established influential ways of representing serene facial expressions, refined bodily proportions, religious gestures and narrative figures. Later sculptural centres in northern, eastern and western India drew on these approaches while developing distinct regional traditions.

Prelims focus

  • The Sarnath Buddha is an important example of Gupta-period sculpture.
  • The celebrated seated Sarnath Buddha dates to the late 5th century CE.
  • Sarnath sculpture is associated with delicate, transparent-looking drapery.
  • The Sarnath teaching Buddha is identified through dharmachakra mudra and a wheel with deer.
  • The Varaha relief is in Cave 5 at Udayagiri, Madhya Pradesh.
  • Trap: Heavy robe folds are characteristic of Gandhara, not the refined foldless treatment typical of mature Sarnath sculpture.

[Sources: NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class XI, Chapter 4, printed pp. 31–32 and 52–53, and Chapter 6, 'Temple Architecture and Sculpture', printed pp. 72–73; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Udaigiri Caves', India's Tentative List entry no. 7046, submitted 8 July 2026, consulted 23 November 2026.]

title: Gupta Sculpture: Sarnath Buddha, Religious Iconography and Stone Reliefs

body:
The emergence of regional styles

Between approximately the 7th and 13th centuries CE, sculptural traditions developed in different parts of India under the patronage of regional dynasties, religious institutions and local communities.

The appearance of a sculpture depended partly on the properties of the available stone, the skills of the artisans and the traditions associated with a region. Differences are visible in bodily proportions, ornaments, poses, narrative arrangement and the depth of carving.

Pallava sculpture: Mamallapuram

The Pallavas were important patrons of sculpture and architecture in Tamil Nadu. Mamallapuram or Mahabalipuram became a major centre during the 7th century CE.

Its famous open-air relief is commonly called Arjuna's Penance or Descent of the Ganges. These names reflect different interpretations of the composition.

The relief depicts numerous figures, including ascetics, animals and celestial beings, around a prominent natural rock setting. Particularly noteworthy are the carefully modelled elephants and other animals.

The Pallava site also contains the Pancha Rathas, demonstrating how large architectural and sculptural forms could be created by carving existing rock.

Chalukya sculpture: Aihole, Badami and Pattadakal

The Early Chalukyas developed important rock-cut and structural monuments in present-day Karnataka. Major centres include Aihole, Badami and Pattadakal.

At the Ravana Phadi Cave in Aihole, an important sculptural composition represents Nataraja accompanied by the Saptamatrikas, the group of 7 mother goddesses.

Chalukyan sculpture often combines slender bodies, elaborate ornaments and rhythmic movement. Regional styles also show interaction between northern and southern architectural and sculptural conventions.

Rashtrakuta sculpture: Ellora

The Rashtrakutas are especially associated with the monumental Kailasa Temple, Cave 16, at Ellora in Maharashtra. The temple was excavated from a mass of living rock during the 8th century CE.

Unlike a structural temple assembled from separate stone blocks, the Kailasa complex was produced by removing large quantities of rock to leave the desired architectural and sculptural forms.

One of its most famous reliefs shows Ravana shaking Mount Kailasa. The sculptors used deeply projecting figures, overlapping bodies and contrasting levels of relief to create a dramatic composition.

Chandella sculpture: Khajuraho

The Chandellas patronised the temples of Khajuraho in Madhya Pradesh, particularly during the 10th–11th centuries CE.

The temples are known for elaborate sandstone carvings of deities, attendants, musicians, dancers, animals, decorative forms and mithuna figures, which represent embracing couples.

The sculptors created graceful postures and richly ornamented bodies. Figures often project strongly from the surrounding wall surface, producing an impression of movement.

The Lakshmana Temple and Kandariya Mahadeva Temple are important examples.

Khajuraho's sculpture is not limited to erotic subjects. Religious figures, decorative motifs and scenes representing different aspects of human experience form major parts of the temple programmes.

Hoysala sculpture: Belur, Halebidu and Somanathapura

The Hoysalas developed an especially intricate stone-carving tradition in Karnataka during the 12th–13th centuries CE.

Important centres include Belur, Halebidu and Somanathapura. Many temples use relatively workable soapstone, which allowed artisans to carve detailed jewellery, clothing, animal figures and ornamental bands.

Hoysala temples are also recognised by complex, often star-shaped plans. The projecting walls provide numerous surfaces for sculptural decoration.

The Hoysaleswara Temple at Halebidu is particularly noted for its profuse carvings and detailed animal friezes.

Pala and Sena sculpture in eastern India

The Pala tradition developed in Bihar and Bengal, especially during the 9th–11th centuries CE. Related developments continued under the Sena rulers.

The region produced Buddhist, Hindu and Jain sculptural images in stone and metal. Black or dark stone, intricate ornaments and carefully arranged figures are important features of many surviving works.

Nalanda became a major centre of Buddhist artistic production. Its sculptural tradition developed from earlier Gupta influences while incorporating local forms and increasingly elaborate representations of Buddhist figures.

Material and regional identity

Materials help in identifying sculptural traditions, but should not be used as the sole test. For example, red sandstone strongly suggests certain Mathura works, while soapstone is important in Hoysala sculpture. Yet different materials could be used within the same region, and artistic styles changed over time.

Prelims focus

  • Pallavas: Mamallapuram, Tamil Nadu; Arjuna's Penance or Descent of the Ganges relief.
  • Early Chalukyas: Aihole, Badami and Pattadakal in Karnataka.
  • Rashtrakutas: Kailasa Temple, Cave 16, Ellora.
  • Chandellas: Khajuraho temples in Madhya Pradesh.
  • Hoysalas: Belur, Halebidu and Somanathapura; intricate soapstone carving.
  • Trap: Ellora's Kailasa Temple is rock-cut, while Khajuraho's major temples are structural sandstone monuments.

[Sources: NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class XI, Chapter 6, 'Temple Architecture and Sculpture', printed pp. 74–101; NCERT, Our Pasts-II, Class VII, Chapter 5, 'Rulers and Buildings'.]
